tasks.locator: Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
tasks.source_read: publisher full text (HTML), NEJM, https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMsa1211128 (Supplementary Appendix and disclosure forms, both PDFs, not opened)
tasks.extracted: Never smoked: fewer than 100 cigarettes in a lifetime. People who had stopped smoking: at least 100 cigarettes in a lifetime and none in the previous 5 years. People who had stopped within 5 years before death were counted as currently smoking, the authors' step against reverse causation. Age-stratified Cox models adjusted for education (3 levels), alcohol (4 levels) and body-mass index (3 levels), weighted to the survey; adding race made no material difference (not presented). Survival from 25 to 80 combines age-specific ratios, smoking prevalence and 2004 US death rates; scaling the survey's death rates up to national rates did not materially change the absolute differences (data not shown).

tasks.extracted: Acute toxicity data on nicotine are limited and come from three sources: animal studies, trials of nicotine as a medicine and poisoning reports. The animal studies do not adequately characterize acute toxicity; the medicine trials use amounts chosen because they are thought to be subtoxic; poisonings are documented, but the literature has not been assessed systematically for the relation between amount and effect; the commonly quoted human fatal oral amount is poorly documented (the chapter's literature search found no source for it). The Summary says nicotine has known acute toxicity and that poisoning is possible from ingesting nicotine-containing products. No amounts are used in this claim.

tasks.locator: Chapter 5 › Health Consequences of Nicotine Exposure › Reproductive Health Outcomes, 3rd paragraph; Fetal Growth Restriction, 1st paragraph; Preterm Delivery, 1st paragraph; Stillbirth, Perinatal Mortality, and Sudden Infant Death Syndrome, 1st paragraph; Summary, 1st paragraph
tasks.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML, Surgeon General 2014 (surgsmoke50): chapter 1 (Major Conclusions, Chapter Conclusions, Table 1.1), chapter 5 (all sections) and chapter 3 (grading); other chapters not read
tasks.extracted: Inference about nicotine alone in pregnancy comes from studies comparing prenatal smokeless tobacco with prenatal smoking (smokeless products do not expose people to combustion products but all contain nicotine; Swedish snus has lower levels of some toxicants) and from randomized trials of nicotine therapy in pregnant women. Fetal growth: smokeless tobacco shows only modest contributions to lower birth weight; Swedish population study 1999 to 2010, snus and small-for-gestational-age term births, adjusted odds ratio 1.21 (95% CI 1.02 to 1.43), smaller than for smoking (the smoking figure is printed as 2.27 with an interval of 2.62 to 2.91, so it is not quoted); a trial of 250 pregnant women found no difference in quit rates or saliva cotinine between nicotine-patch and placebo arms but a birth weight 186 g higher (35 to 336) in the patch arm, possibly due to less smoking; the chapter reads these as supporting a modest role for nicotine in fetal growth restriction. Preterm delivery: smoking linked to a 27% higher risk (Shah and Bracken 2000, as cited); rises of similar size with snus and with smoking in Sweden. Stillbirth: higher risk with smokeless tobacco in India and Sweden; in the Swedish study the smoking-related stillbirth risk fell markedly when antenatal bleeding and small-for-gestational-age deliveries were excluded while the snus risk stayed the same, which the chapter reads as both involving nicotine, with other factors also contributing in smoking. Summary: the evidence supports a key role for nicotine in the adverse effects of smoking on reproductive health, including preterm delivery and stillbirth.

tasks.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML, Surgeon General 2014 (surgsmoke50): chapter 1 (Major Conclusions, Chapter Conclusions, Table 1.1), chapter 5 (all sections) and chapter 3 (grading); other chapters not read
tasks.extracted: Smoking in adolescence is associated with lasting cognitive and behavioural impairments, including effects on working memory and attention, but causal relationships are hard to establish with potential confounding; animal studies show that nicotine in adolescence affects the brain differently from exposure at other ages; the concluding paragraph calls adverse effects of adolescent exposure on cognition likely, while the graded conclusion is only suggestive (the graded level is used here); effects after adolescence and young adulthood are unknown.

tasks.locator: Chapter 5 › Health Consequences of Nicotine Exposure › Cancer › Genotoxicity, 1st paragraph; Experimental Animal Studies for Carcinogenicity, 1st and 4th paragraphs; Human Studies, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Summary, 1st paragraph
tasks.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML, Surgeon General 2014 (surgsmoke50): chapter 1 (Major Conclusions, Chapter Conclusions, Table 1.1), chapter 5 (all sections) and chapter 3 (grading); other chapters not read
tasks.extracted: Genotoxicity data are mixed (most assays negative, two positive). Animal studies mostly do not show nicotine alone to be tumour-causing (one exception: sarcomas in one mouse strain); nicotine promotes tumours in some models but not those driven by tobacco-specific nitrosamines; the animal findings do not support nicotine as a complete carcinogen. People: very little data; the Lung Health Study is the only source on long-term nicotine replacement (5,887 enrolled, 3,220 followed 7 more years, 75 lung cancers, no link with replacement use; short follow-up); smokeless tobacco raises the risk of cancers of the mouth, oesophagus and pancreas, less than smoking, and does not raise many smoking-related cancers, which suggests nicotine may not have a strong tumour-promoting effect, tempered by the different route (oral rather than inhaled). Summary: insufficient data to conclude that nicotine causes or contributes to cancer in humans; possible oral, oesophageal and pancreatic risks; substantial experimental evidence that nicotine is active in carcinogenic mechanisms; in vitro data suggestive but not supported overall by the most recent animal studies.

tasks.locator: Chapter 5 › Health Consequences of Nicotine Exposure › Cognitive Function › Effects of Nicotine on Cognitive Function in Healthy Adult Smokers and Nonsmokers, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Tobacco Industry Influence, 2nd to 4th paragraphs; Evidence Summary, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Implications, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
tasks.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML, Surgeon General 2014 (surgsmoke50): chapter 1 (Major Conclusions, Chapter Conclusions, Table 1.1), chapter 5 (all sections) and chapter 3 (grading); other chapters not read
tasks.extracted: Acute nicotine has modest cognition-enhancing effects in adults who smoke during withdrawal (the evidence summary adds adults who do not smoke); a meta-analysis of double-blind placebo-controlled studies (nicotine given mainly as replacement products) found enhancement in 6 of 9 performance domains in people who do not smoke and in people who smoke and had been abstinent for up to 2 hours; less is known about long-term exposure. The chapter reports that a 1997 review found authors acknowledging industry funding reported positive findings on nicotine and cognitive performance almost exclusively while authors without industry funding reported positive and negative findings, that in studies of smoking and Alzheimer's disease the pooled odds ratios without industry funding were neutral or showed higher risk with smoking while industry-affiliated studies showed lower risk, and that industry ties are often not disclosed in articles citing such work. The report calls for information on the risks of long-term nicotine exposure compared with smoking and with no tobacco use at all, says long-term nicotine use may have adverse consequences for those exposed and harms the developing fetus, names cancer, cardiovascular and neurocognitive outcomes as of concern, and states that all tobacco products contain toxicants and so all tobacco product use poses some health risks.

tasks.locator: Chapter 1 › Methodologic Issues › Misclassification of Secondhand Smoke Exposure, 3rd to 6th paragraphs; Misclassification of Secondhand Smoke Exposure › Use of Meta-Analysis, 3rd to 6th paragraphs; Confounding, 1st to 4th paragraphs (figure captions not counted)
tasks.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML, Surgeon General 2006 (rptsmokeexp): chapter 1 in full; chapters 2 to 10 not read
tasks.extracted: Random misclassification of exposure tends to reduce the apparent effect; classifying some people who currently or formerly smoked as people who never smoked would push the lung cancer association upward when smoking clusters between spouses, but the analyses cited cannot fully explain the observed increase this way; because exposure has been widespread there are almost no truly unexposed people, so estimates may be biased downward. Meta-analysis is used with the recognition that the uncertainty around pooled estimates may exceed what conventional statistics show, because of biases in or selection of the studies; one analysis of 37 studies suggested that smaller studies gave higher risks, another found little evidence of publication bias, and efforts to find possibly missing studies are said to have yielded little or nothing that would alter published conclusions (the printed sentence is garbled); the pooled results were not decisive for the causal conclusions. Confounding: adults with more exposure tend to have less healthful lifestyles in US and UK surveys (how far this generalizes is uncertain), socioeconomic status may lie on the causal pathway, and confounding matters more as associations get weaker.

tasks.extracted: The main exposure is current exclusive cigar smoking (or cigar and/or pipe); people who currently smoke cigarettes are excluded so as to isolate cigars; 'primary' means no history of cigarette or pipe smoking and 'secondary' means such a history; in CPS-I people in the secondary group were about twice as likely to report inhaling (42.0% against 21.6%); the reference group is people who never smoked or never used tobacco; results are given descriptively as 'mortality ratios' (standardized mortality ratios, hazard ratios, incidence rate ratios and odds ratios, some calculated by the reviewers) because exposure definitions, dose categories and adjustment vary.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
tasks.source_read: PMC full text PMC4408600 (all sections and Tables 1 to 27 as text; Figure 1 and Additional file 1 not read)
tasks.extracted: The authors prioritize primary cigar smoking in the larger cohorts. Outcomes significantly associated with primary cigar smoking in one or both CPS cohorts: all causes, oral, oesophageal, pancreatic, laryngeal and lung cancers, coronary heart disease and aortic aneurysm; dose trends for the four cancers; raised risks with no inhalation, particularly in CPS-I, which they link to cigar smoke being inhaled regardless of self-report (one cited study); raised but mostly non-significant ratios at 1 to 2 cigars a day. In CPS-I the risks were considerably higher for secondary than for primary cigar smoking for lung cancer (6.29 against 2.1) and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (4.39 against 1.42), which they attribute to different inhalation and to lung damage from earlier cigarette smoking.

tasks.source_read: PMC full text PMC4408600 (all sections and Tables 1 to 27 as text; Figure 1 and Additional file 1 not read)
tasks.extracted: As cited by the review and not re-read: the International Agency for Research on Cancer concluded in 2004 that cigar and/or pipe smoking causes cancers of the lung and upper aerodigestive tract and found evidence that it is causally associated with cancers of the pancreas, stomach and bladder. In the EPIC cohort (incident cancers, median follow-up 9 years), 1,451 people had smoked only cigars (74% currently, 26% formerly); among those currently smoking only cigars the hazard ratio was 3.9 for lung cancer and 3.5 for upper aerodigestive tract cancer, the risk of any tobacco-related cancer (1.6) was still raised when no inhalation was reported, and the combined risk of lung, upper aerodigestive tract and bladder cancers rose with cigars a day and was raised across small, medium and large cigars. In an INHANCE pooled analysis of 19 studies (13,935 cases and 18,691 controls), people who never smoked cigarettes but ever smoked cigars had an odds ratio of 2.54 (95% CI 1.93 to 3.34) for head and neck cancer, rising with frequency and duration, while the ratio was not raised among people who had ever smoked cigarettes.

tasks.source_read: PMC full text PMC4408600 (all sections and Tables 1 to 27 as text; Figure 1 and Additional file 1 not read)
tasks.extracted: Limits the authors state: studies largely of white men in North America and Europe who smoked cigars in the 1960s or earlier; the large cigar predominates, unlike today's market; limited data for stomach, colorectal and liver cancer; studies often underpowered at the lowest exposures. They call for contemporary cohorts with women, non-white people and younger adults, with detail on cigar type, number a day, inhalation, years of smoking and biomarkers. Not stated by the authors but visible in the tables: most estimates are adjusted for age alone, and the tables contain mismatches in cohort labels, cause-of-death codes and citations (listed on the study card).

tasks.locator: Abstract › Conclusions; Conclusions, 1st paragraph
tasks.source_read: PMC full text PMC4408600 (all sections and Tables 1 to 27 as text; Figure 1 and Additional file 1 not read)
tasks.extracted: The authors conclude that cigar smoking carries many of the same health risks as cigarette smoking, that risks vary with cigars a day and inhalation, and that some risks can be as high as or exceed those of cigarette smoking (the main-text conclusions add that this holds especially at the highest amounts and levels of inhalation; the abstract does not). The review tabulates no estimates for people who smoke cigarettes and excludes them by design, so this is not a result shown by its tables.

tasks.extracted: For scale only, not a comparison made by either study: in the Jha cohort of US men interviewed in 1997 to 2004, adjusted hazard ratios for current cigarette smoking against fewer than 100 cigarettes in a lifetime were 2.8 (99% CI 2.4 to 3.1) for all causes and 14.6 (9.1 to 23.4) for lung cancer, at ages 25 to 79; in that survey 52.7% of men who currently smoked reported 20 or more cigarettes a day. The era, adjustment (age, education, alcohol, body-mass index), comparison group and amount smoked differ from the cigar cohorts.
